text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Well, Koreans take recycling very seriously. We separate almost everything. Plastic goes in one bin, paper in another, cans and glass in another. Food waste has its own special bag, and everything else goes in a paid trash bag. If you throw your trash in the wrong place, your neighbors will notice! In my apartment complex, there's a special recycling area with big colored containers. Everyone brings their stuff there once a week. People recycle all kinds of things: plastic bottles, cardboard boxes, newspapers, and cans. Before you throw out a plastic bottle, you have to take the label off and rinse it out. It's a lot of work, honestly. But it's become a habit, and I think it's a good one. Korea is actually one of the best countries at recycling.

Honestly, my family is the recycling boss in our house. We have a small corner on the balcony with separate boxes for everything. Every night, I take out the trash and the recycling. That's my job. At first, I was terrible at it. I'd throw a greasy pizza box in with the paper, and my family would catch me right away. "That's not paper!" I felt like a kid getting scolded. Now I know the rules. Mostly, we recycle plastic bottles, cardboard boxes, and cans. And since I drink so much coffee, I try to use my own tumbler instead of paper cups. I feel a little guilty about all those coffee cups I've thrown away. In our apartment, recycling day is Tuesday evening. If I forget, we get stuck with a full balcony for a week!

Back when I was a kid, recycling was very different. We didn't have those colored bins. Instead, we reused things as much as we could. For example, we took empty soda bottles back to the corner store, and the owner gave us a little money for each one. My friends and I used to collect them and trade them for candy! We also saved old newspapers and metal cans in the corner of the yard. Every few weeks, an old man with a truck came by, shouting, "Old newspapers! Scrap metal!" He'd weigh them, and sometimes he gave us a bar of soap or a roll of toilet paper. As for regular trash, we burned it in the yard. That's not allowed anymore, of course. It wasn't as organized as it is now, but I'd say we wasted less.

My favorite place in Korea is Gangneung. It's on the east coast, and it's about a four-hour drive from my city, but it's totally worth it. There are two reasons I love it. First, the sea. The East Sea is so much clearer and bluer than the one in the south. Second, the coffee! There's a street called Anmok Coffee Street, where there are dozens of cafes lined up along the beach. As a coffee lover, it's like heaven. I usually grab a cup, walk along the sand, and watch the waves. My friends and I go there almost every year. We also love the pine forests and the fresh seafood. The raw fish there is amazing. Honestly, I could live there, if it weren't for my job!

Before a trip, I have a routine, mostly because I'm a bit of a worrier. I make a checklist a week ahead. The first thing is the reservations: the hotel and the car. Then I check the weather forecast, so I know what to pack. For clothes, I take a jacket, comfortable shoes, and a couple of extra shirts. Then the gadgets: my phone charger, a power bank, and headphones. I always forget the charger! Once, I got to the hotel and realized I'd left it at home. I had to buy a new one at a convenience store. I also make a list of cafes I want to visit. That's the most important part for me. Finally, I put snacks and water in the car. And last, I do a final check of the stove and the windows. My friends say I'm worse than a flight attendant!

I remember a family trip to Sokcho and Seoraksan when I was about ten. There were nine of us in one van: my parents, six cousins, and me! It was so crowded, and I got stuck in the middle seat. My cousins sang the whole way, and I got terribly carsick. My mom had to stop the van twice. It was a total mess! But when we finally got to the mountain, I forgot everything. The rocks and trees were beautiful, and the air was cold and fresh. We rode a cable car for the first time. I was terrified, so I held on to my oldest cousin's arm. In the evening, we ate fried fish by the sea, and the sunset was gorgeous. I fell asleep on the way home. Funny enough, it's the trip I remember best from my childhood.

What I like most about my phone is the music app. I have a huge playlist, and I carry it everywhere. I can't tell you how many times it's saved my day. Whenever I'm stuck in traffic, or I'm waiting in a long line, I just plug in my earbuds. Suddenly, I'm somewhere else. I made a playlist called "My Favorite Band Collection", and it has every song by my favorite band. When I'm stressed at work, I take a ten-minute break, put on a song, and I'm good to go. I also like that the app recommends new songs based on what I listened to. I've found a lot of great stuff that way. To be honest, I'd probably go crazy without it. My phone is basically my pocket concert hall.

My first phone was a flip phone, believe it or not. I got it when I started college, and I was so proud of it. It had a tiny black and white screen, and a little antenna on top. I could only make calls and send text messages. Each message had a limit of about 80 characters, so I had to write short and sweet. I also played a snake game on it for hours. The battery lasted for almost a week, though. That's something I miss! My current phone is totally different. It has a huge touch screen, a great camera, and I can do almost anything on it. But I have to charge it every night. And I'm glued to it. Back then, I'd leave the phone at home and not worry. Now I feel lost without it. It's convenient, but it's kind of a trade-off.

Yes, and it was a nightmare. A while ago, I had a business trip to Seoul. I had to catch an early flight, and I used my phone as a boarding pass. The night before, I forgot to charge it. At the airport, I looked at my phone, and the battery was at 3 percent. I thought, "I'm fine, it'll last a few minutes." Then, right at the gate, it died. My boarding pass was gone! I started to panic. The line was getting longer, and people were looking at me. Luckily, a staff member was very kind. She printed a paper boarding pass for me. Then she even let me charge my phone at the counter. I was so relieved. Of course, as someone who works in IT, I felt embarrassed. Since then, I always carry a power bank, and I have a printed backup. Lesson learned!

Hey, thanks for inviting me to the park this weekend. I'm really up for it! I just have a few questions. First, which park are we going to?. Okay, I know that one. What time do you want to meet?. Sounds good. Are we going to just walk around, or do you have something planned?. Oh, nice. Is it okay if I bring another friend?. Of course. And what about food? Should we bring our own lunch, or buy something there?. Got it. I'll bring some coffee, as always. Also, what should I wear? Is it going to rain?. Alright, see you on Saturday!

Hey, I have some bad news about this weekend. I just checked the park's website, and it turns out they're closing the park for renovations. They're working on the walking paths and the playground. It'll be closed all week, so we can't go. I'm so sorry. I know we were both looking forward to it. But don't worry, I have a few ideas. First, there's a bigger park by the sea in the next town. It's about 20 minutes away, and it's open. Second, how about we go to a nice cafe with a garden? I know a great one. Third, if the weather's bad, we could go to a movie or play some screen golf. What do you think?. Okay, great. It's a plan! And the coffee is on me.

Yes, and it was a bit of a scary one. When my friend's little boy was about five, we took him to a big amusement park with a huge lawn. It was crowded, and there were kids running everywhere. My friend and I were taking photos of the scenery, and when we turned around, the boy was gone. My heart dropped. We looked everywhere, and I felt sick. I ran around yelling his name, and my friend went to the information desk. About ten minutes later, a staff member called us. They'd found him, and he was standing in front of an ice cream truck with a big smile. He said, "I wanted to buy ice cream!" I hugged him so tight. I was angry and relieved at the same time. We bought three ice creams. Since then, I never let go of his hand. It was a bad experience at the time, but now we can laugh about it.

Okay, I'd like to compare rock music and classical piano music. They're like night and day, but they have a few things in common. Let me start with the differences. Rock is loud and full of energy. It has electric guitars and drums, and it makes me want to move. I listen to it when I'm driving or when I need a boost. Classical piano, on the other hand, is calm and quiet. It's just one instrument, and the sound is soft. I listen to it when I'm reading or working. If I listened to rock while reading, I'd never finish a page! But they also have a lot in common. Both of them tell a story without many words. Both can make me feel something deep, like sadness or joy. And both need real skill. A guitar solo or a piano piece takes years of practice. So I'd say they're two sides of the same coin. One is for fun, and the other is for peace. I need both.

There are a few music gadgets that are really popular right now. The first one is wireless earbuds, especially the ones with noise canceling. They're special because they block out the noise around you. On the subway, you can't hear a thing except your music. I have a pair myself, and I honestly can't live without them. The second one is a Bluetooth speaker. They're small and cheap, but the sound is surprisingly good. People take them to the beach or the park. Kids these days carry one everywhere. The third is a smart speaker. You just say, "Play my favorite song", and it does. It's like having a personal DJ. And lately, record players have come back, which surprised me. Young people love the old, warm sound. I think they're popular because they're convenient, and everyone wants music anywhere, anytime.
